name: table
title: Table
description: The sheet's .ds-rows and .ds-row: a panel-coloured stack separated by hairlines, closed by a softer one. The sheet builds its rows out of a CSS grid with fixed column widths, because it is laying out one dashboard; a table is a table, so the surfaces are what get borrowed.

/**
 * The field anatomy, shared by every control that wears it — `TextField`,
 * `SearchField`, and the textarea, select, checkbox and radio still to come.
 *
 * Only the styling lives here. Each component defines its own slot components,
 * thin as they are, so that its docs and manifest describe its own API rather
 * than pointing at another component's.
 */

/**
 * The three control sizes. `size` is set once on the field and travels as two
 * custom properties rather than through React context: the control, and any
 * affix inside it, are ordinary descendants of the field, so inheritance already
 * does the work. It also means a one-off override is just a utility on the
 * element rather than a new prop.
 */
export type FieldSize = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'

export const FIELD_SIZES: Record<FieldSize, string> = {
  sm: '[--field-control-h:2.25rem] [--field-control-text:0.8125rem]', // 36px / 13px
  md: '[--field-control-h:2.75rem] [--field-control-text:0.875rem]', // 44px / 14px
  lg: '[--field-control-h:3.25rem] [--field-control-text:0.9375rem]', // 52px / 15px
}

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-field`: legend, control, then the hint that explains it.
 *
 * The `font-size` here is what the control and any affix inherit. It sits on the
 * field rather than on the input so it still reaches an affix, which is the
 * input's sibling — a `cap`-sized icon would otherwise match the page's font
 * instead of the field's.
 *
 * The two border properties are published here for the same reason `Checkbox`
 * publishes its own: read-only lives on the field root, while the border it changes
 * is on the input, and a group variant cannot win that cascade — see the note on
 * `INPUT`. Declaring them here means the input only reads them, and the ordinary
 * cascade decides, because `[data-readonly]` plainly outranks the bare declaration.
 */
export const FIELD = [
  'group flex flex-col gap-2 [font-size:var(--field-control-text)]',
  '[--field-border:var(--color-input)]',
  '[--field-hover:var(--color-border)]',
  // Read-only is not disabled: the value is the whole point of the field, so it
  // keeps full-strength text. Only the affordances go — a quieter hairline, and no
  // brightening on hover — because there is nothing here to invite a click on.
  'data-[readonly]:[--field-border:var(--color-border-soft)]',
  'data-[readonly]:[--field-hover:var(--color-border-soft)]',
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-affix` wrapper. `Group` exists for one case: an affix is
 * positioned against the control, but the field also holds the legend and the
 * hint, so an affix anchored to the field would centre on all three.
 * Wrapping the control gives the affix the right box — and it stays opt-in, so a
 * plain field has no extra element at all.
 *
 * The two `:has()` rules are here for the same reason: the room an affix needs is
 * padding on the input, and the group is what can see both of them. The input
 * itself never has to know it has neighbours.
 */
export const GROUP = [
  'relative flex w-full',
  'has-[[data-slot=icon-start]]:[&>[data-slot=input]]:ps-10.5', // 42px, per the sheet's search field
  'has-[[data-slot=icon-end]]:[&>[data-slot=input]]:pe-14', // 56px, per the sheet's trailing unit
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`: 12px, uppercase, letterspaced, white 70%.
 *
 * The required marker is drawn from the field's own `data-required`, so the label
 * never has to be told and the asterisk cannot drift out of sync with
 * `isRequired`. The input already carries the native `required`, so this is the
 * visual half of the same fact.
 */
export const LABEL = [
  'text-[12px] uppercase tracking-[0.04em] text-muted-foreground',
  "group-data-[required]:after:ms-1 group-data-[required]:after:text-destructive group-data-[required]:after:content-['*']",
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-input`.
 *
 * The resting hairline is what identifies the control. The sheet gives
 * `.ds-input` a transparent border and leaves the panel-2 fill to do the job, but
 * that fill is 1.23:1 on the dark page and 1.17:1 on the light one, so the field is
 * nearly invisible as a boundary in both. `--input` is the smallest
 * hairline that clears the 3:1 a control boundary needs on each.
 *
 * Hover has to *strengthen* it rather than replace it: the sheet's hover is white
 * at 25%, which is now weaker than the resting line and would erase it.
 *
 * `outline-none` on focus suppresses the *browser's* ring, which is what the
 * sheet's `.ds-input:focus { outline: none }` is really doing. Chrome gives a
 * focused text input its `:focus-visible` ring at `outline-style: auto` regardless
 * of React Aria's attribute, so leaving it alone means a blue UA ring on a teal
 * system. Focus is then the border alone — adding the shared 3px-offset ring here
 * would draw two parallel teal hairlines with a gap, which reads as a fault.
 * `Button` can carry that ring because the edge it repeats is a solid fill.
 */
export const INPUT = [
  // **The corner is a token now, and `rounded-md` is the control step of its scale.** Pulse's own
  // `--radius` is `0`, so the sheet's square field is unchanged here; a theme that sets a radius
  // moves every control in the library at once. See the radius note in `docs/theming.md`.
  'w-full font-mono rounded-md border border-(--field-border)',
  'h-(--field-control-h) px-3.5',
  'bg-muted text-foreground placeholder:text-foreground/35',
  'transition-[border-color,background-color] duration-(--duration-fast) ease-pulse',
  // Focus and invalid stay literal, so they outrank the published border and always
  // win — including on a read-only field, which is still focusable and still the
  // field the caret should be able to reach.
  'data-[hovered]:not-data-[focused]:border-(--field-hover)',
  'data-[focused]:outline-none data-[focused]:border-primary',
  'data-[invalid]:not-data-[focused]:border-destructive',
  // The browser already knows when someone has left a field invalid, so the state needs no
  // "touched" class and no blur listener — it only needed a rule. Same line in `TextArea`.
  'user-invalid:not-data-[focused]:border-destructive',
  'data-[disabled]:cursor-not-allowed data-[disabled]:opacity-40',
  // Read-only gets the cursor and nothing else that dims it. `opacity` here would
  // take the *value* down with it — at 40% the text measures 3.42:1, under the 4.5:1
  // body text needs, so the one thing the user came to read becomes the thing they
  // cannot.
  'group-data-[readonly]:cursor-not-allowed',
].join(' ')

/** The sheet's `.ds-hint`: 12px, tighter tracking, white 55%. */
export const HINT = 'text-[12px] tracking-[-0.5px] text-foreground/55'

/**
 * The sheet paints its error state yellow, because the original design had only
 * two accents and yellow was the nearest thing to a warning it owned. That does
 * not carry over here: `--warning` is this system's `secondary` button, so
 * errors would be the same colour as a secondary action. The error state uses
 * `--destructive`, the danger hue, and keeps the sheet's flex so an icon can be
 * dropped in front of the message.
 */
export const ERROR =
  'flex items-center gap-1.5 text-[12px] tracking-[-0.5px] text-destructive'

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-affix__unit` and `.ds-affix__icon`: pinned to the control's
 * box, vertically centred, and never a click target — the affix is decoration, and
 * a pointer-events-owning overlay would swallow clicks meant for the field. Sized
 * in `cap` like `Button.Icon`, so one icon works at every field `size`.
 */
export const ICON = [
  'absolute inset-y-0 z-10 grid place-items-center pointer-events-none',
  'text-foreground/70',
  '[&>svg]:block [&>svg]:h-[1.5cap] [&>svg]:w-auto [&>svg]:shrink-0',
].join(' ')

/** The sheet insets both affixes 14px from their edge. */
export const ICON_POSITIONS = {
  start: 'start-3.5',
  end: 'end-3.5',
} as const

export type IconPosition = keyof typeof ICON_POSITIONS

/**
 * The load-more sentinel's shared parts, so `GridList.LoadMore`, `Table.LoadMore` and `Tree.LoadMore` are
 * one recipe in three collections rather than three drifting copies — the same reason `field.ts` and
 * `date.tsx` exist.
 */

/**
 * A quiet centred strip at the foot of a list, where the next page arrives.
 *
 * It is deliberately the least conspicuous thing in the component: a page boundary is a seam in the data,
 * not an event, and a reader scrolling past should see the list continue rather than a control.
 */
export const LOAD_MORE =
  'flex items-center justify-center gap-2 p-4 text-[11px] uppercase tracking-[0.08em] text-foreground/45'

/**
 * The spinner, in the sentinel's own colour.
 *
 * `motion-safe`, so a reader who has asked for less motion gets a still one rather than none of it.
 */
export function LoadMoreSpinner() {
  return (
    <span
      data-slot="loader"
      aria-hidden="true"
      className="size-3 border border-foreground/30 border-t-fg motion-safe:animate-spin"
    />
  )
}

docs:
The sheet's `.ds-rows` and `.ds-row`: a panel-coloured stack separated by hairlines, closed by a softer one. The sheet builds its rows out of a CSS grid with fixed column widths, because it is laying out one dashboard; a table is a table, so the _surfaces_ are what get borrowed. ```tsx Monitor Status fra1 · Frankfurt Up
``` | Slot | React Aria | Notes | | -------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | `Table` | `Table` | `aria-label`; `selectedKeys`, `disabledKeys`, `selectionMode` | | `Table.Header` | `TableHeader` | The column headings | | `Table.Column` | `Column` | `isRowHeader` marks the column whose cell names the row | | `Table.Body` | `TableBody` | Takes `renderEmptyState` | | `Table.Row` | `Row` | Its `id` is what `selectedKeys` and `disabledKeys` speak in | | `Table.Cell` | `Cell` | One cell | ### The header is the table's, not the sheet's The sheet has **no table header at all**. Its rows are a dashboard grid where each cell holds its own 12px uppercase label above its value, so the row carries its labels with it. A real table says them once at the top instead, and the headings take the sheet's _quieter_ legend — 11px, spaced, 45% — rather than the full-strength treatment a row's own label gets. Row headers are the exception: the column marked `isRowHeader` is the row's identity, so it keeps full strength and everything else sits at 75%. That is styled off `[&[role=rowheader]]` on the cell, so which column identifies the row is decided once, on the column, and the styling cannot drift from it. ### Selection is a slot, and React Aria drives it `Table.Selection` is a `Checkbox` carrying `slot="selection"`. React Aria finds it by that slot and does everything else: the one in the column heading becomes select-all, and it goes **indeterminate** on its own when some rows are chosen — the `mixed` state a table needs and a plain checkbox does not have. ```tsx Monitor fra1 · Frankfurt
``` **Do not pass it `isSelected` or `onChange`** — the table supplies both through the slot, and passing them fights it. The header checkbox is labelled "Select All" by React Aria and each row's from its row header, so there is nothing to name. A selection column is a gutter, not a column: it holds a control and a heading that is itself a control, so `Table.Column` and `Table.Cell` narrow themselves to 12 units when they contain one — `has-[[data-slot=selection]]` — rather than making every table spell that out. ### No numeric variant The sheet gives its figures 16–20px, and its headline figure `--warning`. That belongs to its dashboard, where a number _is_ the point of the row. In a table it is one column of many, and a table of yellow figures is a table where nothing stands out. Pass a `className` when a column really is the point. ### A row's hover cannot be tested, so there is no story for it React Aria _does_ set `data-hovered` on a row, and it is the "correct" RAC way to style one. But it wires that to **pointer enter, which does not bubble** — so a pointer over a cell does not shade its row, and `user-event` fires its events on the target alone. The native `:hover` is no better: browsers apply it from real input only, and a synthetic event is not that. So the row's hover is the native pseudo-class — matching the sheet's `.ds-row--hover:hover` — and there is deliberately no Hover story. A story that asserts the row is opaque at rest and calls itself "Hover" would pass while testing nothing, which is worse than not having it. ### Two things the roles turned out to be - **React Aria gives a table the _grid_ roles**, not the table ones: `role="grid"` on the element, `gridcell` on the cells. So query `gridcell`, not `cell`, or the query finds nothing and the failure reads like a missing body. - **The empty state is a full-width `rowheader`.** `renderEmptyState` on the body renders a single cell with `colspan` and `role="rowheader"`, so `queryAllByRole('rowheader')` is 1 on an empty table, not 0. Assert on the message being visible and on there being no `gridcell`s. ## Resizable columns: `Table.Resizable` + `Table.Resizer` ```tsx Monitor {/* … */} …
 ``` | Slot | React Aria | Notes | | ----------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | | `Table.Resizable` | `ResizableTableContainer` | The scroll container. Required — see below | | `Table.Resizer` | `ColumnResizer` | Inside a `Table.Column`, on its trailing edge | **The two are one feature, not two props.** A `ColumnResizer` _throws_ without the container — React Aria's own message is _"Wrap your `` in a `` to enable column resizing"_. The container walks up to the first scrollable element and measures that, which is why it has to be the thing that scrolls, and why it carries `overflow-x-auto`. Column widths come from the column: `defaultWidth`, `minWidth`, `maxWidth`, or a controlled `width`. The grip shows its hairline on hover and turns **teal while the drag is live** — the accent for a genuinely active state, the same rule a selected row follows. It sits _over_ the column's trailing edge (absolute, `-end-px`) rather than taking a share of it, so widening a column never eats the neighbouring cell's padding. **Drag is the interaction and it is a pointer sequence** — pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup. A single `click` asserts nothing about it. Verified directly in the browser: dragging the Monitor grip 117px took that column from 220 to 337 and left its neighbours at 140 and 120. **The story does not assert the drag, and that is deliberate.** `userEvent.pointer` could not drive React Aria's resize here — with absolute `clientX`/`clientY` (which are accepted and then ignored when a `target` is given) or with target-relative `x`/`y` — while a real mouse does. Rather than ship an assertion that silently proves nothing, the story asserts what the runner can actually demonstrate: the column's width coming from `defaultWidth`, the grip's `role="presentation"` wrapper carrying a `type="range"` control with the column's accessible name, and the outline regression below. ### The focus ring here could never draw This column's class list carried `outline-none` next to a `data-[focus-visible]:outline-1` ring. Because `outline-none` sets Tailwind's **shared** `--tw-outline-style` — the very property every `outline-` utility reads back — the ring was unreachable: the element reported `outline-width: 1px` with `outline-style: none`. It is now a **transparent outline at rest** (`outline-1 -outline-offset-2 outline-transparent`), and `Table`'s `Resizable` story asserts exactly that, at rest, where `solid` with a transparent colour is correct and `none` is the failure. `GridList`'s row had the identical bug and the same fix; its rows now compute `2px solid` with a transparent colour. ## `Table.Footer` — the closing row ```tsx Fleet 3 monitors 98.99% ``` **A footer is not a body row that happens to be last.** It is the table's conclusion — the totals, the count, the average — and it is the one row a reader arrives at deliberately rather than scanning past. So the separation line goes _above_ it rather than below, and its type is a step quieter (`text-foreground/60`) than the data, which is the same relationship the header has at the other end. It holds `Table.Row`s like the body does, because it is the same collection machinery underneath. It renders a real **``**, after the `tbody` — and that is the assertion the story makes, because a footer drawn as a last body row looks identical and is not one. A `tfoot` written before `tbody` is legal HTML and still renders last, so the story checks the actual group order: `THEAD, TBODY, TFOOT`. ## `Table.LoadMore` — the row that asks for the next page The same sentinel as `GridList.LoadMore`, on the same shared recipe (`loadMore.tsx`). It only works inside a virtualized collection, draws nothing until `isLoading`, and **React Aria renders nothing at all for it when idle** — so a test asserts the element is absent rather than that it is empty. The mechanism, and the end-to-end proof that it fires on scroll, are in `gridlist.md` and `virtualizer.md`; this component is that machinery in another collection.
